Turf between pavers in Kissimmee, Florida

Turf between pavers ties a driveway, walkway or patio together with a green line instead of loose rock or bare joint sand. In Kissimmee the turf itself still runs the usual $8–$18 a square foot, but a narrow strip prices near the top of that range because the edge work, not the area, takes the crew's time. Most jobs finish in a day.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Where turf between pavers works, and where it doesn't

A paver and turf installation succeeds or fails at the joint between the two materials, not inside either one alone. Turf between pavers earns its keep in specific spots: driveway ribbon turf down the center where tires never track, stepping stone turf filling the gaps between treads on a path through the yard, grid pavers with artificial grass over a parking pad, or a checkerboard patio alternating paver squares with turf squares off the lanai. It reads as intentional, not as a lawn that failed.

It also solves a problem Kissimmee homeowners run into with real grass in these spots: a strip a few inches wide between pavers dries out fast in full sun, and Toho Water Authority's two-day watering schedule rarely keeps it alive. A wide-open area next to the hardscape is a different job. A 600 sq ft side yard is cheaper and simpler as one piece of lawn turf than as ten narrow ribbons, so we reserve the paver-and-turf approach for the spots the hardscape pattern actually creates. Driveway wheel paths are a poor fit for the same reason turf ribbons work everywhere else: turf laid where tires roll gets crushed and stained with oil, so the green strip belongs in the center or along the border, never in the tracks.

Four ways we lay turf and pavers together

The layout decides almost everything else about a job: strip width, how the edge gets held, and where the water goes. These four patterns cover most of what comes up in Osceola and south Orange County yards.

Turf-and-paver layouts and their build notes
LayoutTypical widthEdge treatmentDrainage note
Driveway ribbon turf8–18 inThe paver course on both sides doubles as the nailing edgeCrowned slightly so runoff sheds toward the paver joints, not the garage
Stepping stone turf path4–8 in between treadsTucked tight to the paver's chamfered edge, nailed into the base beyond itBase has to drain as fast as the turf or the strip becomes a sponge between dry pavers
Grid pavers with artificial grass2–4 in cell openingsNo separate edge; the paver cell holds the turf plug in placeBuilt for infiltration, so the base under the cells stays open rather than compacted solid
Checkerboard patioFull paver-size squares, 12–24 inBender board or a mortared edge around each turf squareEach square carries its own slight crown so water doesn't pool in the pile

Widths are typical for residential jobs; a site visit sets the exact number against the paver pattern you have or are choosing.

One layout, two base materials

Pavers and turf don't actually want the same base material, which surprises people expecting one uniform layer under everything. Pavers sit on a dense-graded aggregate, sized to lock together tight enough to carry a tire's point load without shifting. Turf's base has to do close to the opposite: the state synthetic turf standard requires a washed, open-graded crushed rock or crushed concrete subgrade under turf, sized and washed so fines don't bind it into a crust that stops water from passing through. Run one material under the other and either the turf floods or the paver bearing surface goes soft.

What stays continuous is the layout, not the aggregate: one finished grade set for the whole area before either material goes down, one drainage plan, and an edge restraint that ties the two base types together at the joint instead of leaving a gap.

  1. One grade, cut once. We set the finished elevation for the whole area before either material goes down, so the paver's dense-graded base and the turf's washed, open-graded base meet at the same finished height.
  2. Two base materials, kept separate. Paver zones get a dense-graded aggregate compacted for bearing; the turf strip gets a washed, open-graded crushed rock or crushed concrete base per the state standard, with a fabric or edge to keep the two from migrating into each other.
  3. Edge restraint goes in first. A paver edge restraint, a bender board, or the paver course itself is set and checked for line before a single roll of turf gets cut.
  4. Turf is cut long, then trimmed tight. Strips are cut a little wide and trimmed to the paver edge on site, because even a good hardscape job is never perfectly straight.
  5. Fastened into the base, never into the paver. Nails or adhesive anchor into the turf's own base material beside the paver, so the turf can be lifted for a repair without disturbing the hardscape.
  6. Infill matched to the strip width. A narrow ribbon gets a slightly heavier rate of clean silica sand or a coated sand so the blades stand up instead of leaning flat toward the paver's shade line.

How turf between pavers is priced

Turf between pavers doesn't fit a clean per-square-foot number, because most of the cost is edge, not area. The turf itself still falls in the usual Central Florida range, $8–$18 a square foot installed, but a paver-and-turf job prices toward the top of that range or gets quoted as one flat price for the whole strip. A crew still shows up, compacts a base and sets an edge restraint whether the ribbon covers 400 square feet or 40.

What pushes the number up: narrow widths, which mean more linear feet of edge per square foot of turf; curves that follow a paver pattern instead of a straight run; matching an existing paver color and joint width exactly; and coordinating a schedule with a separate hardscape crew when the pavers aren't part of the same job. What holds it down: a straight run, a strip wide enough to read as its own material rather than a sliver, and pavers that are already in and level so we're not correcting someone else's grade first.

What Florida sun, storms and sand do to a paver-and-turf job

Pavers and turf don't handle heat the same way, and that matters when they sit inches apart. Concrete and clay pavers hold the sun's heat and release it slowly, so the blades along that edge often run hotter than the middle of an open lawn; a light paver color and a quick hose rinse bring both surfaces down together (installer heat measurements). Central Florida's summer storms, which can drop one to three inches of rain in an hour, are the bigger risk: a narrow strip with a paver lip on both sides has nowhere to shed water sideways, so the crown and the base's drainage matter more here than on a wide-open yard.

Kissimmee's fine native sand settles unevenly under two different base materials compacted to two different specs, which is why the subgrade underneath both gets graded and firmed the same way before either aggregate goes down, rather than treating one side as an afterthought once the other is finished. The state standard also caps how hard that native soil can be compacted, since packing it too tight under the turf hurts percolation. Near a live oak, root flare can lift a paver course and the turf edge riding against it at the same time; if the layout falls inside the tree's drip line, the state's synthetic turf standard requires a certified arborist to sign off before we build there.

Permits, HOA review and the driveway apron

A driveway ribbon or a front-walk path is, by definition, visible from the street, which puts it outside the protection homeowners get under F.S. 720.3045; that statute only stops an HOA from restricting turf that can't be seen from the frontage or a neighboring lot (the statute text). In communities such as Celebration or Reunion, expect an architectural review application for a front-yard paver-and-turf project even though a fenced backyard version of the same idea might not need one. What a Florida HOA can and can not restrict covers that split in more detail, and the permit guide lists what each local office asks for when pavers and drainage are both part of the scope.

What a rushed paver-and-turf job looks like two summers later

The tell is almost always at the edge. Turf nailed straight into the paver instead of into the base pulls the fastener loose the first time the paver shifts on its own bedding sand, and the strip lifts in a wave along one side. A joint width that wasn't held consistent looks fine from the porch and uneven from the driveway, especially where two crews worked from two different chalk lines. Infill that wasn't matched to a narrow strip washes into the paver joints during the rainy season, leaving the turf thin and the joints stained.

A base compacted only under the turf, with loose sand left under the pavers, settles at a different rate, so the paver edge ends up a quarter-inch proud of the turf within a year, a lip that catches a stroller wheel or a bare foot. This guide covers the same failure mode where turf meets a hard surface generally.

Keeping the joints clean

Rinse the strip with a hose along with the rest of the yard; a paver-and-turf ribbon collects more windblown grit than an open lawn because it's narrow and often runs along a hard edge that channels debris. Brush the pile against the grain a few times a year so it doesn't lie flat toward the paver, the direction both water and foot traffic push it. Keep an eye on the paver joints themselves separately, since the sand there is a different material with its own refresh schedule than the turf's infill.

After a named storm, walk the full edge. A lifted corner caught early is a small repair, and the state's anchoring requirement exists precisely because wind gets under an unanchored edge before rain does.

Who is the best turf and paver installer near me?

That's the right question to ask before signing anything, and the honest answer is that you can't tell from a finished photo. Ask three things: whether the quote lists one compacted base spec for the whole area instead of a vague "standard prep," whether the edge restraint is named outright (paver, bender board or spike edge) rather than assumed, and whether the crew has actually tied turf into an existing paver layout before, since that's a different skill from either trade alone. A contractor who answers all three without hesitation has likely done it more than once.

Questions people ask

Can turf go between pavers I already have, or do the pavers have to be new?

Existing pavers work fine as long as they're level and the joint is at least a couple of inches wide. We check the paver's bedding for firmness first; if it's already settling, that gets corrected before turf goes in next to it, or the fix won't last.

How wide does a turf strip between pavers need to be?

There's no hard minimum, but strips under about three inches are hard to seam cleanly and tend to look like caulk rather than grass. Four to eight inches reads as an intentional design line; anything wider starts behaving like its own small lawn.

Will turf between pavers fade a different shade than a nearby lawn?

It can, if the two are different products or ages. We try to match pile height and color family when a paver strip sits near an existing turf lawn, though a strip installed years apart from the lawn will show some difference the way any two turf ages do.

Does turf between pavers need its own drainage?

It needs to drain into the same overall plan the pavers do, even though the aggregate under the turf is a different, washed and open-graded material than the paver base. Both are graded off the same layout, so water moving through the turf has somewhere to go instead of pooling against a paver lip.

Can turf go inside grid pavers on a driveway that carries car weight?

Yes, that's what grid pavers with artificial grass are built for. The rigid paver grid carries the wheel load, and the turf plug inside each cell sits on the same washed, open-graded base the state standard requires for any turf, so the cell stays permeable instead of packing solid under traffic.

How do you keep infill from washing into the paver joints?

Matching the infill rate to the strip width helps, along with keeping the turf's finished height slightly above the paver surface so water sheds off the blades before it reaches the joint sand. On very narrow ribbons we sometimes skip infill and rely on a denser, self-standing pile instead.

Is a paver-and-turf driveway ribbon covered by the same Florida turf law as a backyard lawn?

The state's synthetic turf standard applies to the material and how it's installed regardless of where on the lot it sits. The HOA-visibility statute is what changes: a driveway ribbon is visible from the street, so it doesn't get the same protection from architectural review that a fenced backyard strip would.
